extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of aesthetics, philosophers, and creative writers studying the principles of beauty and taste
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting/assessing the aesthetic qualities that constitute 'beauty' across senses (sight, touch, hearing) as laid out in a philosophical essay; intended to guide judgments of beauty in nature and art. Emphasizes sensible qualities (size, smoothness, variation, color, motion, etc.) and distinguishes beauty from utility, proportion, and perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and habit (custom) alter pleasure but do not constitute beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Use and habit make objects indifferent by habituation: continual possession deadens pleasure, while absence produces unease; thus habit-based attachment is distinct from genuine aesthetic pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: habitual visits to a place produce discomfort if missed though they gave little pleasure while present; snuff-taking becomes automatic and its removal causes unease. Anti-pattern: mistaking the discomfort of absence or dependence for evidence of true beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROPORTION NOT THE CAUSE OF BEAUTY
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that proportionality or measured ratios are the cause of beauty is rejected: proportion often coincides with beauty but is neither necessary nor sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/contra: many perfectly proportioned animal parts are not considered beautiful (elephant trunk, wolf form); beauty may appear where no assignable proportion exists. Anti-pattern: assuming that because proportion and beauty co-occur, proportion causes beauty (sophism of the fly).

rubrics_metrics.name: FITNESS NOT THE CAUSE OF BEAUTY
rubrics_metrics.description: An object's utility or the fitness of its parts for an end does not itself constitute beauty; fitness yields approbation rather than the passion of love or immediate aesthetic pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: functional features (swine snout, pelican bag, porcupine quills, elephant trunk) are admirable for use but not beautiful. Note: in works of art fitness/proportion operate on the understanding and produce approval, but not the imaginative affection that defines beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: PERFECTION NOT THE CAUSE OF BEAUTY
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfection, as such, is not the object of love or beauty; highest perfection can produce reverence or awe rather than the tender affections associated with beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sublime virtues (fortitude, justice) cause admiration/terror rather than love; feminine affectations of weakness illustrate that perceived imperfection or delicacy often heightens loveliness. Anti-pattern: equating moral or formal perfection with loveliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: THE REAL CAUSE OF BEAUTY
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty primarily consists in certain positive sensible qualities in bodies that act mechanically on the human mind through the senses, producing immediate affective responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This leads to examining specific sensible qualities (size, smoothness, variation, color, etc.) across the senses to identify what produces the passion of love or tenderness distinct from rational approbation.

rubrics_metrics.name: BEAUTIFUL OBJECTS SMALL
rubrics_metrics.description: Beautiful objects are, comparatively, small — diminutives are the usual objects of love and tenderness, whereas great objects tend to provoke admiration (the sublime) rather than love.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Linguistic evidence: diminutive epithets frequently signal affection; examples: little birds, small animals, endearing 'little' prefixed to loved things. Use this to distinguish between responses of love versus admiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: SMOOTHNESS
rubrics_metrics.description: Smoothness is a central constituent of beauty; almost nothing considered beautiful is rough or rugged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: smooth leaves, polished furniture, smooth skin. Smoothness can outweigh other qualities: a rugged surface destroys beauty even where form is otherwise good. Anti-pattern: sharp angles, sudden projections, and rugged textures reduce or abolish perceived beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: GRADUAL VARIATION (non-angular, continuous lines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parts of beautiful objects continually vary direction in a gradual, flowing manner — lines are 'melted into one another' rather than straight or angular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a dove's outline, the insensible swell from neck to breast. Anti-pattern: angular figures and sudden directional changes (sharp right lines) are generally ugly; variants of the 'line of beauty' must be smooth and insensible in change.

rubrics_metrics.name: DELICACY (appearance of fragility)
rubrics_metrics.description: An air of delicacy or slight fragility enhances beauty; robustness and overt strength are prejudicial to loveliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: delicate plants (myrtle, jasmine), graceful animals (greyhound), and the perceived delicacy in women. Caveat: pathological weakness or ill-health that spoils other conditions (color, surface variation) is not beautiful.

rubrics_metrics.name: BEAUTY IN COLOR
rubrics_metrics.description: Colors of beautiful bodies are clean, fair, and mild rather than dusky, muddy, or intensely strong; if colors are vivid they are diversified and gradated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred colors: light greens, soft blues, weak whites, pink reds, violets; complexion should mix colors with soft gradation so bounds are hard to fix. Anti-pattern: one strong glaring color without gradation. Examples: variegated flowers, peacock necks where brilliance is diversified.

rubrics_metrics.name: SUMMARY CHECKLIST OF SENSIBLE QUALITIES (RECAPITULATION)
rubrics_metrics.description: A concise recapitulation of the sensory properties upon which beauty depends: (1) comparatively small, (2) smooth, (3) variety in direction of parts, (4) parts melted into one another (non-angular), (5) delicate frame, (6) clear and bright but not glaring colors, (7) if glaring colors exist, diversified with others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this list as a checklist when judging visible beauty; these properties operate by nature and are less liable to caprice than other supposed standards (proportion, utility).

rubrics_metrics.name: THE PHYSIOGNOMY
rubrics_metrics.description: Physiognomy (facial expression) contributes significantly to human beauty; the face must be expressive of gentle and amiable qualities that correspond with softness and delicacy of form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manners influence countenance; to form complete human beauty ensure the expression suggests tenderness/amiability in harmony with outward form.

rubrics_metrics.name: THE EYE
rubrics_metrics.description: The beauty of the eye consists chiefly in clearness, a slow/languid motion, and a harmonious union with neighboring facial parts (no strong deviation into exact geometry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: we like clear transparent things (diamonds, clear water). Motion: slow and languid is preferable to brisk; eye also gains beauty from expressiveness (qualities of mind). Anti-pattern: dull/muddy 'water' of the eye or jerky/brisk movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: UGLINESS
rubrics_metrics.description: Ugliness is, in general, the opposite of beauty — composed of contrary qualities — but it is not simply the opposite of proportion or fitness and can coexist with those.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ugliness may coincide with the sublime when combined with terror; do not conflate lack of proportion/fitness with ugliness automatically. Use the earlier positive criteria to diagnose ugliness (ruggedness, angularity, gross colors, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: GRACE
rubrics_metrics.description: Gracefulness pertains to posture and motion: it requires no appearance of difficulty, slight inflection of the body, composure of parts, roundness, and delicate, unencumbered motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grace is closely related to beauty but specifically applies to movement and pose. Examples: classical statues (Venus de Medicis, Antinous). Anti-pattern: motions showing effort or awkward sharp angles are ungraceful.

rubrics_metrics.name: ELEGANCE AND SPECIOUSNESS
rubrics_metrics.description: Elegance is smoothness and polish combined with a degree of regular shape (regularity distinguishes it from mere beauty); very large compositions with such qualities become 'fine' or 'specious' rather than merely beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction when evaluating art or furniture: delicate, regular works of art that imitate no determinate natural object fall under 'elegant'; grand scale shifts the affect toward 'fine' or 'specious'.

rubrics_metrics.name: THE BEAUTIFUL IN FEELING (touch)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures of touch that correspond to visual beauty arise from slight resistance (smoothness) and softness, continual but gradual variation of surface, and absence of sudden changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Touch-specific notes: softness and slight resistance increase pleasure; moderate warmth is pleasant; sudden application or sharp changes are disagreeable (startle effect). Analogize tactile qualities to visual criteria when describing textures in writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: THE BEAUTIFUL IN SOUNDS
rubrics_metrics.description: Beautiful sounds are clear, even, smooth, and weak; the beautiful dislikes loudness, shrillness, harshness, deepness, and rapid/abrupt variety or quick transitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Musical analogues: Milton's 'linked sweetness long drawn out' exemplifies the beautiful in sound (melting voice, winding bouts). Use slow, linked, gently varying musical language; avoid rapid modulations that excite mirth or tumult rather than a sinking/languorous affection.

rubrics_metrics.name: DISTINGUISH IMMEDIATE AFFECT (love) VS RATIONAL APPROBATION
rubrics_metrics.description: When judging beauty, differentiate immediate imaginative affection (love, tenderness) from cold approbation produced by reason (understanding that admires fitness/proportion). True beauty strikes before reason and requires no knowledge of use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical test: does the object move the passions prior to reflection (beauty) or does it only win the intellect's approval once its purpose or mechanism is known (fitness/proportion)? Use this to separate aesthetic value from functional merit.
